description:
This is our review of the AMD RX 6800 XT video card, looking at RDNA2 and the reference cooler vs. the RTX 3080, 3090, 3070, RX 5700 XT, & more. Includes Smart Access Memory tests.
Sponsor: Crucial Ballistix RAM (Amazon: https://geni.us/eykEA)

Watch our AMD RX 6800 XT tear-down here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0s7bOaa6X9E

Find the AMD RX 6800 XT on Amazon, in theory: https://geni.us/DfaMM
Find the NVIDIA RTX 3080 cards on Amazon (also in theory): https://geni.us/ABpmb6I
And the AMD Ryzen 9 5900X on Amazon: https://geni.us/ZN7myl
Gigabyte X570 Master on Amazon: https://geni.us/X4Ed

GPU TESTING METHODOLOGY EXPLAINER: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-P7-ML-bPCE
Grab a GN Modmat here: https://store.gamersnexus.net/products/modmat

Our AMD RX 6800 XT reference video card tear-down will be posting later today, hopefully alongside the AMD RX 6800 (non-XT) review. As a reminder, the RX 6800 XT competes directly with the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 cards (theoretically at $650 for the XT vs. $700 MSRP for the 3080). The RX 6800 non-XT competes with the RTX 3070 (with the 3070 running theoretically cheaper). Our review of the AMD RX 6800 XT looking at thermal design, cooling, noise levels, gaming performance, Smart Access Memory on vs. off performance, AMD Ryzen vs. Intel performance, ray tracing (RTX/DXR) benchmarks vs. NVIDIA, RDNA2 overclocking behaviors, and more. This is one of the densest-packed reviews we've published lately, and we barely finished it before embargo lift. More to come in short order. Our pressure testing and flatness testing will be pushed into a secondary piece focusing entirely on thermals, as this review ran long enough as is. PCIe 4 vs. PCIe 3 doesn't make much impact on performance, as we showed previously with the RTX 3080, and so any AMD vs. Intel CPU differences are primarily resultant of the higher performance of AMD (particularly at 1080p). Our benchmarks include 4K, 1440p (2560x1440), and 1080p for the RX 6800 XT vs. RTX 3080, et al. Smart Access Memory testing includes the requisite Ryzen 5000 (5900X) CPU, X570 board, and RX 6000 GPU. NVIDIA is working on its own competing feature, but they didn't launch it in time for this review.

The best way to support our work is through our store: https://store.gamersnexus.net/

Like our content? Please consider becoming our Patron to support us: http://www.patreon.com/gamersnexus

I have an RTX 3080 on the way, and I am waiting on CPUs to be in stock to replace my 3930k (probably a 5600 but I may even swing higher). Virtual Desktop for Quest 2 works better on Nvidia because the encoding is better, according to the developer of the app. I am literally getting this card to play a highly upscaled Half Life Alyx wirelessly! My GTX 1070 really struggles when I try to play the full resolution Quest 2 wirelessly, so I am gifting the card alongside a 144hz 1080p monitor to my 12 year old nephew for Christmas.

Using VR FPS tools, I am going to see just how little CPU matters for VR, since it's use-case is EVEN MORE GPU bound than 4k pancake gaming is. I am even starting to wonder if it makes sense to get a new CPU. I'll test it in a few days when I have a 3080. I just wish a pro like you had the time to make sense of this, since some misinformation floats around the community about this topic. Many people into VR don't even know how little the CPU matters for it.

That being said it is at best mediocre cooler when compared to good AIB models or NVIDIA's Founders Edition. Though please remember that this video was posted just at the beginning of shortages. comments.text: Well, the thing is, nVidia's ASIC method of RT is always going to mean Ampere will handle more BVH data, and handle it faster than AMD's hybrid texture processor based solution. So if a game is optimized for RDNA2, it will simply mean it's not utilizing RT as much as it could if it were optimized for Ampere. AMD had a huge opportunity to really outdo nVidia's rasterisation performance, because RTG didn't have a die space penalty of using ASIC's that won't be doing work in normal rasterisation. Unfortunately, as Radeon fans are now very accustomed, RTG shot themselves in the foot, and wasted the opportunity by going with GDDR6 + a large cache instead of HMB2 + a large cache. I suspect they did this because they knew even if they threw absurd amounts of bandwidth at their hybrid RT solution, they still wouldn't match nVidia's ASIC performance with DLSS and they'd be stuck with the manufacturing cost of using HBM2. So, they cheaped out on the manufacturing cost as much as they could, and instead of delivering a card with significantly more rasterisation performance, they manage to match nVidia in rasterisation while falling hugely behind in RT performance. It's honestly pretty scummy behavior from AMD, because the GPU market is clearly set up as a duopoly, and AMD is taking advantage of the market by manufacturing their cards as cheaply as possible, while only slightly undercutting nVidia's GPU's. As someone who has bought primarly AMD/ATi GPU's for the last 20 years, I'm tired of the behavior from both AMD and nVidia.
comments.author: @K31TH3R

comments.text:
@K31TH3R  Bit unfair there - AMD have jumped up hugely in performance, which is a fairly important point. I've never owned an ATI/AMD graphics card at all (and this is going back near 30 years, when I first bought a PC with a Matrox Millennium), I'm now in a position where I can genuinely consider taking a Radeon instead of the RTX.

Yes, I'm slightly disappointed by the lower bandwidth memory on the Radeon cards. But then I'm also disappointed that the 3080 has less total memory than the 2080. That total memory hasn't been a big deal before now, but there are a couple of titles that are pushing the memory  And if developers start pushing more/larger textures because of the console architectures, having a bit more memory might be useful - depending on whether you lean towards higher fidelity or higher performance.

As you say (and I said), it all comes down to what developers optimise for. And the presence of RDNA2 in both the PS5 and Series X is going to have a huge influence on that. The primary platforms for developers to optimise ray tracing implementations for are the consoles - there will be thousands in the market in a very short space of time, whereas the PC "only" has the very expensive Turing, and RDNA2 / Ampere cards are in short supply.

It's no guarantee, but it just seems likely that if developers spend most of their time optimising the implementation for PS5 / Series X, that those settings will also carry over to the PC -meaning that Turing will have a fighting chance, and both RDNA2 and Ampere should work quite well with some ray tracing features implemented.

How many are going to also add additional settings/features that really make use of Ampere? When they haven't really rushed to embrace Turing, I don't have a huge amount of confidence that they are going to put much effort into targeting a(nother) card that people can't get hold of.
comments.author: @GrahamTriggsUK

comments.text:
@GrahamTriggsUK  Oh, don't get me wrong, as someone who loves AMD GPU's (my daily driver is a 5700 XT) I'm absolutely thrilled with their huge leap in performance and am happy they're more than competing in many situations.
I suspected, since the earliest leaks of the RX 6000 series and their RT design patents, that AMD would be attempting to muddy the waters of what "the fastest GPU" means, and they'd do this by releasing a card with much faster rasterisation performance which falls short in RT. But for that tactic to win people over, the rasterisation performance needed to be a full generation ahead of nVidia instead of roughly matching it.
RDNA2 is clearly a more efficient architecture than Ampere as well as long as you're not looking at RT.
It really comes down to "do you want the best rasterisation performance? Or do you want the best RT performance?" Because it seems we now have two specialized GPU's.
Personally, I care more about rasterisation performance than RT performance, so AMD is looking great to me, but it seems most people disagree with me on that front.

comments.text: @GingerLess000  Wafer prices have gone up significantly too. Yet the die size for GPUs have stayed roughly the same, whereas the die size for CPUs have gotten smaller because they haven't grown in transistor count to catch up with the shrink factor. The asking price for a TSMC standard process 7nm wafer is ~$10,000 (AMD probably get a bit better prices than that though), but you only get 104 big navi dies if the yield is 100% (which it absolutely isn't). @somethinglikethat2176  The second sentence of your statement; "Even without a pandemic and record demand big product launches selling out is the rule rather than the exception." actually validates the point I am trying to make. These new RX 6000 series, along with the nVidia 30 series, Sony, MSoft - all of these products will sell out regardless of the channels which they release these products for sale. 

So, why would companies whose revenue streams are into the billions elect to release these products as a free for all? Simply put, they do not care enough to invest more time and money into figuring out a way to get their products into legitimate consumers' hands, and their top lines will not see an immediate 1:1 trade-off on said investment, so they opt to not do it. It really is as simple as that.

As it pertains to 'global supply chains; my gripe is not with stock levels and yes I am fully aware of the fact items sell out, that's what happens. Where they have gone wrong is their piss-poor execution of product launches and the lack of giving a shit about their customers; they are all fully okay with catering to scalpers and bots.

So, we then have YTers such as GN, Linus, Jay, etc who let these companies legitimately receive 100's of thousands of dollars worth of marketing and advertising in exchange for what, an early sneak peek at their product? Yet here they all still are, pushing their content out as soon as possible to be the first one out so they can capture the attention and views. If any of these shills had a spine, they would not release their product reviews until the company actually has a means to get these products to real, breathing humans. But yeah, Steve will try and say how he's "not a shill" - you're a shill for the ad dollars, Steve. All of them are.

comments.text:
@jonfromsyracuse  GN releasing a review does not somehow magically endorse the card or the company's decisions during release day. As for "investing more time and money", pretty much every method people have suggested would be "EZ Fixes!!!" to get them to more real customers is easily defeated by minor bot changes or scalpers just buying the card as an average person. Limit it to 1 card per household? Not gonna stop hundreds of scalpers from scooping up one each or using family member's addresses. Wait till they have enough stock to last a while? It only changes the first few minutes of launch day, since production is happening either way. Nobody's getting their card any quicker.

 I find it nearly conspiracy theory level thinking that Nvidia or AMD don't care about the colossal, overwhelming backlash they've received over availability. Steve and the majority of the techtubers you listed have roasted them over this issue, and I doubt anyone will forget about it for years. The idea that the companies think "Oh well, I'm selling cards either way!" is just nonsense. Hell, imagine an alternate universe in which AMD had millions of cards on launch. We would've seen an enormous swing to Team Red that might have persisted in the market for years after. Nvidia and AMD aren't going to pull punches when it comes to availability and real customers, since whoever manages to get their shit together first and reach "In Stock" status will not only sell the most, but be hailed as a savior (lol) on forums and community recommendations make a massive impact.

As for the last paragraph: Reviewers reviewing things? On a launch day? Yep, they must all be part of the corporate machine, man. They should just not release their reviews alongside the product (you know, like GN did with the 5700xt Red Devil because they literally couldn't buy one) and that'll show those corporations they mean business! /s 

Unless you actually rely on a GPU for work and you require a specific aspect of the new models, believing that the inability to buy one is showing the infinite greed of mankind is a bit much. comments.text:
@enrique6335  I mean, it is better now. Nvidia has had way more time in the oven when it came to software support and extra features. Which means they are going to find themselves more favorable in most titles even from just a driver standpoint. Kinda what happens when almost the entirety of the GPU market is just NVIDIA for multiple generations back-to-back. So for AMD to come in and offer equal to better raw performance against NVIDIA's high end gpu's means that they've made some serious improvements to their architecture.

I've never been one to praise AMD's graphics department, but the 6800xt is absolutely solid competition to NVIDIA, and when almost every PC title doesn't support Ray-Tracing+DLSS, a lot of people are going to find that few hundred dollars in savings in their wallets a compelling option.

Even right now, as GPU supply has started to ease up, the lowest a 3080 goes for is $850 compared to the 6800xt's $700. For a lot of gamers right now that need to get a system upgrade and don't want to wait for next gen to most likely be out of stock yet again, AMD is a great option for graphics cards. And I couldn't imagine myself saying that before RDNA 2. They did it with their CPU department. I never thought my 2020 build would feature an AMD processor and yet they continue to push competition forward. Which even if you don't like their products, there is no denying their competition has benefited performances across all CPU and GPU brands.

I for one am very excited for AMD. I'm not a fanboy, and will absolutely criticize them just as I do for other brands, but they are really coming back in this market with their new leadership and that is very nice. I hope this progress for them continues as RDNA 3 launches between now and early next year.
